- Model consistently underestimates prices in the early part of the 30-day horizon, especially after a recent spike or correction; adjust forecast upward by 1–3% for the first 5–7 days if sentiment is neutral or slightly negative.
- After a sharp price spike (e.g., >80), model tends to overcorrect downward; apply a “lag correction” — delay the downward trend by 1–3 days and reduce slope by 10–20% if sentiment remains flat or mildly bearish.
- When sentiment is positive (even if low, e.g., 0.20), model underreacts to momentum; increase forecast slope by 5–10% for the next 5–7 days to capture sentiment-driven continuation.
- Mean reversion is overestimated — model assumes prices return to prior 10–15-day average too quickly; extend mean reversion window to 20–30 days and reduce slope after 10 days if sentiment is neutral.
- If true outcome shows a “double dip” or “rebound after crash”, model fails to anticipate second leg; add a 2–5 day buffer for rebound in forecast if sentiment turns positive after a dip.
- For horizon >20 days, model tends to overestimate volatility; cap forecast slope at 0.5–0.7% per day after day 15 if sentiment is flat or negative.
